Chapter 166: 0163 Free Ads and Free Games

Before leaving Beijing, Chen Guiliang held a meeting.

First, he listened to a brief report on the work progress of each department.

During this period, everyone's task was simple, but very, very crucial. It was to integrate the newly formed team.

ByteDance, originally with just over 10 people, had suddenly expanded to a little over 100. They didn't know each other, weren't familiar with their own duties, and often made mistakes amidst the chaotic hustle.

Chang Zhongxiang's financial system was basically complete.

Wei Xiaokang, drawing from a host of major companies like Baidu, Sina, Sohu, Tencent, and Alibaba, had created an extremely complex job-ranking system. When the proposal was submitted, it made Ao Yanchen, Guo Feng, Xie Yang, and the others dizzy just looking at it.

Finally, after a discussion among the senior management team, Chen Guiliang made the final decision, settling on a simple and clear 14-level job system. All the sub-levels in the original proposal were eliminated, and promotion criteria would be mainly based on ability and contribution.

Seniority was also counted as a contribution, which is what people commonly refer to as: "even if there's no merit, there's still hard work."

But the weight of seniority wasn't significant; it was very possible for older employees to be surpassed by "juniors."

The company's legal department temporarily had only one legal specialist, Shi Qian, who had been poached from King & Wood Mallesons. This time, he was to be taken by Chen Guiliang to Hangzhou to negotiate the investment.

"Have you guys ever heard of Craigslist?" Chen Guiliang asked.

Everyone shook their heads.

Only Chang Zhongxiang, who was in charge of finance, answered, "The largest free classified advertising website in the United States."

Xie Yang asked, puzzled, "How do free ads make money?"

Chang Zhongxiang said, "It's not entirely free. Job postings in a few major cities are fee-based. But the fees are very low, just a few dozen dollars per ad. When I was working in the States, I bought a used car through Craigslist and even found a girlfriend on it."

Buying a used car was understandable, but what the heck was finding a girlfriend?

Ao Yanchen asked, "Does that... what's-it-called website also have a matchmaking service?"

Chen Guiliang smiled at Chang Zhongxiang and said, "You explain."

Chang Zhongxiang said, "To keep maintenance costs down, that website has no pictures on any of its ads, just dense blocks of text. Users can post ads freely, for selling secondhand goods, renting out houses, recruiting employees... or even for finding a boyfriend or girlfriend."

"Can it break even?" Ao Yanchen asked.

Chang Zhongxiang said, "The website has been around for ten years and doesn't accept investment. It's currently number one in the US, and it even added a BBS function a couple of years ago."

Number one in the US, yet it only had about 20 employees, half of whom were technical staff.

If Chen Guiliang were to do this project, a team of five or six people would be enough to start.

"If Xiaonei wants to increase its profitability, creating a free classifieds website is a good choice," Chen Guiliang said. "And it can also increase user activity on Xiaonei."

"Users posting information about secondhand goods, looking for love, and so on, will all be free. But to prevent malicious ad spamming, we must limit them to one or two posts a day. Free ads will be automatically removed after a certain period to avoid taking up too much server space."

"Additionally, we need to attract businesses to place ads. Pharmaceuticals, health supplements, and the like will be strictly forbidden. Paid ads from businesses can be placed in prominent, front-page positions. The advertising fees should be low, focusing on a model of small profits and quick returns."

"Based on Xiaonei's user base, these ads should primarily be for recruitment. Not just full-time jobs, but more part-time ones, like summer jobs, tutoring, tour guides, and so on. For example, if my son's grades are poor and I want to hire a tutor, I can post an ad here and pay just 10 or 20 yuan a day for it."

Except for Chang Zhongxiang, who had seen Craigslist, the others exchanged glances, expressing serious doubts about this model.

Chen Guiliang continued, "I don't know if it will be profitable, but it will definitely help increase user activity on Xiaonei. If the project fails, we can just consider it an investment in boosting user stickiness. First, let's form a five-person project team to research the specifics of Craigslist."

"Don't treat Craigslist as gospel; a complete copy might not work here. Even Marxist-Leninist thought had to be localized when it came to China. Besides, we can do better than Craigslist! If it gets big, we'll spin it off and operate it as an independent ad website for users across the country."

Ao Yanchen said, "We'll give it a try."

Chen Guiliang didn't interfere too much with the execution; he only needed to provide a clear direction. As for the specifics of how to do it, the employees could use their own initiative.

This was to be Xiaonei's first project after its Series A financing.

Next, Chen Guiliang talked about his upcoming trip to Hangzhou to invest in a game company.

Xie Yang understood immediately.

Guo Feng, however, asked, "Isn't it too risky to invest directly in a game that hasn't even been made yet?"

Chen Guiliang explained, "I believe that game can make money. Because the gameplay and profit model were sold to them by me during my third year of high school. It's actually my game, I just wasn't involved in the subsequent development."

"You were making games in your third year of high school?" Ao Yanchen asked, astonished.

Chen Guiliang laughed, "You guys really think the money I used to start the company all came from royalties and prize money? I made almost 200,000 yuan making games and selling game concepts in my third year of high school. I couldn't be bothered to collect the final payment, otherwise it would have been nearly 300,000."

Everyone fell silent.

His bragging left them speechless.

Xie Yang raised his hand. "I can prove it."

Chang Zhongxiang asked, "Should we inform the director appointed by the investors?"

"I'll tell him," Chen Guiliang said. "But if he raises any objections, I certainly won't accept them."

The director appointed by the investors was not a permanent fixture at the company, only coming for a meeting once a quarter. If a large investment was involved, that director had to be informed, but that was all.

Any reasonably normal founder would not give an investor-appointed director veto power when accepting investment.

At the end of June, Chen Guiliang flew to Hangzhou with a legal specialist and a finance person to discuss the investment.

Tao Chenggang and his three partners warmly welcomed Chen Guiliang's arrival.

His entire team consisted of just over ten people, and they had been working on the game for more than a year. To be honest, none of them felt confident. Their main fear was that their funds would run out, and even if they finished the game, they wouldn't be able to operate it.

Currently, most self-developed games in China had investments under 5 million yuan. It was enough to finish the game, but marketing and promotion funds were sorely lacking—even the major companies were more or less the same, unwilling to allocate too much extra funding to a project.

Seeing that Chen Guiliang had really come to invest, the morale of Tao Chenggang's entire team instantly changed.

Tao Chenggang said to Chen Guiliang, "World of Warcraft has had a huge impact on other subscription-based games. Lineage II, which was extremely popular for a while, has seen its concurrent player numbers plummet since World of Warcraft's open beta. It's a similar story for other subscription games. Our free-to-play strategy is the right one. Yulgang hasn't been affected much."

"So, Yulgang is our biggest competitor?" Chen Guiliang asked.

Tao Chenggang was very confident. "Not a competitor. The gameplay model you gave me is far superior to Yulgang's. Besides, Yulgang is afraid of offending its players, so its crackdown on hacks is weak. I reckon its economic system will collapse sooner or later."

Yulgang's fatal flaws were not limited to its weak anti-hacking measures. There were a host of problems.

The real competitor was Shi Yuzhu's ZT Online!

Using his tactics from selling health supplements, Shi Yuzhu launched a carpet-bombing promotional campaign for ZT Online, setting up over 1,800 branch offices nationwide. Before the game server even went live, he sent out his old health supplement teams to storm the second and third-tier cities across the country, eventually pushing all the way to small county towns.

Once the small county towns were covered, Shi Yuzhu shouted the slogan "Games to the Countryside."

They painted ads on the walls of rural houses, with slogans like "Play online games and get free fertilizer" and "Game cards in every village, gift packs in every town," essentially selling the online game like it was Melatonin.

Then, he was summoned for a talk.

Because the nationwide outcry was deafening, with over 5,000 complaint letters coming in daily.

This was suspected of luring rural left-behind children into playing games!

Such a massive promotional campaign required a huge amount of capital. In Shi Yuzhu's own words: "Throw 100 million US dollars in directly, and have another 100 million US dollars in reserve."

How could Chen Guiliang afford to mess with someone like that?

He could only urge Tao Chenggang to speed up development and seize a share of the free-to-play market first.

Tao Chenggang then led Chen Guiliang to play the game.

"The graphics are too poor, about the same as Legend of Mir," Chen Guiliang said. "After I inject the funds, you should still optimize the art."

Tao Chenggang said, "Okay."

Chen Guiliang personally played the game for an hour and reviewed various game data, mainly focusing on game resources and the economic system.

"Your economic system is too conservative. Regular players will be very poor," Chen Guiliang said.

Tao Chenggang said, "Although there are two systems, free silver and paid gold ingots, I'm worried that too many gold farming studios and hackers will get in and cause the regular players' silver system to collapse."

"Don't be afraid of that. Crack down hard on hackers when you find them, and don't worry about the gold farmers," Chen Guiliang said. "Even the country needs macroeconomic regulation; your game can have it too. Make the economic system more complex, let the free players get rich too. We can achieve common prosperity for all. If the economic system becomes imbalanced, just use in-game means for macroeconomic regulation. You also need to hire someone who understands economics."

Tao Chenggang: "..."

Chen Guiliang said, "I'm not joking."

This kind of approach was also invented by Shi Yuzhu, who constantly performed macroeconomic adjustments on ZT Online's economic system.

Chen Guiliang said, "Regular players need more ways to make money, and more game resources should be made available to them. This isn't a private server. Regular players are very important. Only by keeping them can we keep the big spenders!"

"Opening up too many free resources is tantamount to encouraging gold farming studios," Tao Chenggang said.

"Gold farming studios are not the enemy," Chen Guiliang said.

Tao Chenggang thought about it carefully. Although still a bit hesitant, he finally nodded and said, "I'll give it a try."
